writing.prompt:
Part I Writing (30 minutes)

Directions: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to write an essay on why students should be encouraged to develop the ability to meet challenges. You can cite examples to illustrate your point. You should write at least 150 words but no more than 200 words.
writing.ideas: 审题思路:现象分析类(why 型),解释「为什么要鼓励学生培养应对挑战的能力」。推荐三层论证:① 首段从时代背景切入:不确定性成为常态,挑战不可避免,能力必须前置培养;② 中间段给出两个理由:外部看,职场与生活充满非常规问题,标准答案思维失效;内部看,克服挑战的经验积累成心理韧性(resilience),是自信的真正来源;③ 结尾落到教育建议:学校与家庭应允许学生安全地失败,把挑战设计进成长路径。
writing.model:
We are living in an era when certainty is the exception rather than the rule. Technologies reshuffle industries every few years, and no syllabus can list the problems today's students will face at thirty. That is precisely why the ability to meet challenges deserves to be encouraged, deliberately, from school years onward.
Externally, this ability is what separates people who adapt from people who stall. Graduates who have never wrestled with an open-ended problem often freeze when the first real assignment arrives without instructions. Internally, the benefit runs deeper: each challenge overcome quietly rewrites a student's self-image, turning "I can't" into "I can figure this out." That resilience, not any single certificate, is what carries people through the ambiguous decades of adult life.
Encouraging this ability does not mean throwing students into deep water. It means designing challenges that stretch but do not drown them—research projects that can fail, competitions that can be lost, teams that require negotiation. The point is not to guarantee success, but to make difficulty familiar, so that when the real test comes, the student's first reaction is curiosity rather than fear.
writing.notes: 亮点:① 首句 certainty is the exception rather than the rule 金句式开头;② 中间段 external/internal 双线论证,逻辑清晰;③ turns "I can't" into "I can figure this out" 用引语制造画面感;④ 结尾 stretch but do not drown 对仗,并以 curiosity rather than fear 收尾。加分表达:open-ended problem, rewrites a student's self-image, throwing students into deep water。

listening.intro:
Questions 1 to 4 are based on the conversation you have just heard.

【听力原文】
W: You have been quiet all week. Still thinking about transferring to computer science?
M: Every day. I like literature, but the job statistics are terrifying.
W: And your parents?
M: They would celebrate. But my real fear is that I am running away from something difficult toward something merely profitable.
W: That is a very honest question to ask yourself. Have you tried any programming courses?
M: One introductory course. I enjoyed the logic puzzles, but the debugging sessions drove me crazy.
W: So you know both sides now. What does your advisor say?
M: She suggested I take one more course before deciding, and maybe minor in CS instead of a full transfer.
W: That sounds like a wise middle path. One more semester of data before a lifelong decision.
listening.questions:
1. Why has the man been quiet all week?
A) He failed an exam.
B) He is considering changing his major.
C) He quarrelled with his parents.
D) He lost his job statistics report.

2. What is the man's real fear?
A) That he cannot find any job.
B) That his parents will disagree.
C) That he is escaping difficulty for profit.
D) That programming is too easy.

3. What did the man enjoy in the programming course?
A) The debugging sessions.
B) The logic puzzles.
C) The final exam.
D) The group projects.

4. What did the advisor suggest?
A) Transfer immediately.
B) Drop literature entirely.
C) Take one more course and consider a minor.
D) Quit school for a year.
listening.analysis:
1. B。开头女士问 Still thinking about transferring to computer science,男士沉默一周的原因是在考虑转专业。
2. C。男士自述担心自己是从困难逃向 merely profitable(仅有利可图)的方向。
3. B。他说喜欢 the logic puzzles,但 debugging sessions drove me crazy(调试让他抓狂)。
4. C。导师建议再学一门课再做决定,并可以考虑辅修(minor in CS)而非全面转专业。

listening.intro:
Questions 5 to 7 are based on the passage you have just heard.

【听力原文】
Every January, millions of people resolve to run, read or learn a language, and by February most have quietly quit. Habit researchers say the problem is rarely motivation; it is design. A habit, they explain, has three parts: a cue, a routine and a reward. New Year resolutions usually fail because they change only the routine—"I will run every day"—while leaving the cue and the reward untouched.
In one classic experiment, researchers asked one group to exercise whenever they felt motivated, and another group to exercise at the same time, in the same place, every day. Three months later, the second group had turned exercise into an automatic behaviour, and most were still active a year afterwards.
The practical lesson is to shrink the habit until it is almost embarrassing. Instead of "read fifty pages a night," start with "read one page." Instead of "run five kilometres," start with "put on the running shoes." Tiny habits survive busy weeks, and surviving beats intensity: a small action repeated a hundred times quietly becomes who you are.
listening.questions:
5. Why do most New Year resolutions fail?
A) People lack motivation.
B) They change only the routine.
C) The rewards are too small.
D) January is the wrong month.

6. What distinguished the successful group in the experiment?
A) They exercised with friends.
B) They exercised longer each time.
C) They exercised at a fixed time and place.
D) They felt more motivated.

7. What is the passage's practical advice?
A) Make habits so small they survive busy weeks.
B) Set ambitious goals every month.
C) Reward yourself with food.
D) Exercise only when motivated.
listening.analysis:
5. B。习惯由 cue、routine、reward 三部分组成,新年决心通常只改了 routine,忽略了另外两环。
6. C。实验里成功组每天在固定时间、固定地点运动,使行为自动化。
7. A。文章建议把习惯缩小到几乎难为情的程度(tiny habits),因为能熬过繁忙周的小行动胜过强度。

listening.intro:
Questions 8 to 10 are based on the lecture you have just heard.

【听力原文】
Today's lecture is about municipal waste sorting, a policy now rolling out in cities across China. The stated goal is simple: sort rubbish so that recyclable and hazardous materials leave the general stream. The implementation, as residents of Shanghai discovered in 2019, is anything but simple.
The first lesson from early adopters concerns timing. Cities that gave residents six months of education before fines began saw voluntary compliance rates above eighty percent. Cities that switched on penalties on day one faced protests and quietly relaxed the rules. The second lesson concerns design: sorting works when the bins themselves are well designed. A four-category system with confusing names defeats the purpose; a system with clear labels, convenient drop-off points and, crucially, visible feedback—"your building sorted 92 percent correctly this month"—turns a duty into a mild competition.
The broader significance goes beyond tidiness. Sorting is the cheapest gateway to a circular economy: every tonne correctly separated saves roughly three tonnes of carbon that would otherwise be emitted in producing new material. Small daily acts, multiplied by millions, are how environmental policy actually works.
listening.questions:
8. What was the stated goal of municipal waste sorting?
A) To reduce total waste.
B) To separate recyclables and hazardous materials.
C) To punish careless residents.
D) To build more landfills.

9. What did cities with six months of pre-education achieve?
A) They avoided protests.
B) Voluntary compliance above eighty percent.
C) Higher fines collected.
D) Faster policy rollouts.

10. What does the lecturer say sorting is the gateway to?
A) A cleaner city image.
B) A circular economy.
C) A new industry.
D) A recycling profession.
listening.analysis:
8. B。讲座开头:目标是把可回收物和有害垃圾从一般垃圾流中分离出来。
9. B。先罚款前给了六个月宣传教育的城市,自愿合规率超过百分之八十。
10. B。结尾:垃圾分类是通往循环经济最便宜的入口(the cheapest gateway to a circular economy)。

reading.title: The Case for Learning How to Learn
reading.passage:
Universities have always taught content; very few teach the process of acquiring it. Yet in a labour market where knowledge expires faster each year, the meta-skill—learning how to learn—may matter more than any particular subject. Employers repeatedly report that new graduates know facts but struggle when a problem does not match a textbook template. The missing capability is not intelligence; it is strategy.
Cognitive scientists describe effective learners as people who test themselves constantly. Rereading notes feels productive because the material becomes familiar, but familiarity is not recall. Retrieval practice—closing the book and trying to reconstruct the argument from memory—feels worse and works far better. The same research explains why spacing beats cramming: memories consolidated across several days resist forgetting far longer than memories built in a single night.
A second mark of strong learners is that they treat confusion as information rather than failure. When a paragraph refuses to make sense, weak learners reread it hopefully; strong learners stop, name exactly which sentence broke down, and attack that gap directly. This habit of diagnosing one's own misunderstanding, unglamorous as it sounds, is what separates students who plateau from students who keep improving.
None of this requires talent, only design: quiz yourself, space your sessions, and read your confusion as a map. The classroom teaches what to think; these habits teach how. In an age of change, the second lesson is the one that keeps paying.
reading.questions:
1. What problem do employers report about new graduates?
A) They lack intelligence.
B) They know facts but struggle with non-template problems.
C) They refuse to work overtime.
D) They have poor handwriting.

2. Why does rereading notes feel productive?
A) It improves recall directly.
B) The material becomes familiar.
C) It spaces memory over days.
D) It diagnoses confusion.

3. What does retrieval practice mean?
A) Reading notes repeatedly.
B) Reconstructing material from memory with the book closed.
C) Copying the argument by hand.
D) Discussing with classmates.

4. How do strong learners treat confusion?
A) As a sign of failure.
B) As information to diagnose.
C) As something to ignore.
D) As a reason to reread hopefully.

5. What is the passage's main point?
A) Universities should abandon content teaching.
B) Learning strategies matter more than any single subject.
C) Cramming works for short exams.
D) Talent determines learning ability.
reading.analysis:
1. B。第一段:毕业生知道事实,但遇到不符合课本模板的问题就卡壳,缺的是策略而非智力。
2. B。第二段:重读笔记之所以「感觉」有效,是因为材料变得熟悉(familiarity),但熟悉不等于记得住。
3. B。检索练习指合上书尝试从记忆中重建论证(reconstruct the argument from memory)。
4. B。第三段:强的学习者把困惑当作信息,定位具体断裂的句子并直接攻克(diagnosing one's own misunderstanding)。
5. B。全文主旨:元技能「学会如何学习」可能比任何具体学科更重要,且可通过设计习得。

translation.prompt:
请将以下中文段落翻译成英文:

数字经济正在深刻改变人们的生活方式。移动支付、电子商务和共享出行等新业态,让日常交易变得前所未有的便捷。据统计,中国移动支付用户已超过十亿,小额交易大多通过扫码完成。与此同时,数字化也带来数据安全、隐私保护和老年人「数字鸿沟」等新问题。专家认为,技术创新只有与制度完善同步推进,才能真正造福社会。
translation.reference: The digital economy is profoundly changing the way people live. New business models such as mobile payment, e-commerce and shared mobility have made everyday transactions more convenient than ever before. Statistics show that China has over one billion mobile payment users, and most small transactions are completed simply by scanning a QR code. At the same time, digitalisation has also brought new challenges, including data security, privacy protection and the "digital divide" faced by the elderly. Experts believe that technological innovation can truly benefit society only when it advances in step with institutional improvement.
translation.notes: 要点:①「新业态」译为 new business models,是经济文本的标准说法;②「扫码」用 by scanning a QR code;③「数字鸿沟」已有通行译法 the digital divide,注意加引号后作专有概念;④「造福社会」译为 benefit society,简洁准确;⑤「与……同步推进」译为 advance in step with,比 synchronize 更正式自然。
